title: Atonement: How the Cross Saves
lead: The Bible says that Jesus' death deals with sin and brings people back to God, and uses many pictures for how: a sacrifice, a ransom, a victory, a payment, a cleansing. The church has never settled on one explanation, and the main teachings (ransom and victory, satisfaction, penal substitution, moral influence) are held by different traditions, often together.

sections.b: The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) is the center: the high priest sprinkled the blood of a bull and a goat on the atonement lid of the ark and sent the second goat into the wilderness. Leviticus 17:11 says the blood makes atonement by means of the life in it. The Passover lamb protects Israel's firstborn, and Isaiah 53 describes a servant who bears the sin of many.

Jesus says he came to give his life as a ransom for many. Paul calls him the place of atonement (Romans 3:25), says God made him sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21), and says he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Colossians speaks of a victory over the powers, and Hebrews of a better sacrifice. First John says he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
sections.refs: Mark 10:45; Romans 3:25; Romans 5:9–11; 2 Corinthians 5:19–21; Galatians 3:13; Colossians 2:13–15; Hebrews 9:11–15; 1 John 2:2; 1 John 4:10; 1 Peter 2:24

sections.b: Romans 3:25 and 1 John 2:2 use the Greek hilasterion and hilasmos. Translators have rendered them "propitiation" (turning aside God's anger), "expiation" (removing sin) or "atoning sacrifice." C. H. Dodd argued for expiation; Leon Morris, John Stott and J. I. Packer for propitiation. The Bible's own use of the word for the atonement lid of the ark, the place where sin is covered over, may bring both senses together.
